description.summary: how bright the backdrop behind a translucent surface is

protocol.description:
A client that draws see-through (glass) surfaces over the desktop can't know what shows through them: the wallpaper, a window moving behind, another layer. Fixed text colours that read over one backdrop don't read over another.
This protocol lets the compositor tell a client how bright the backdrop behind one of its surfaces is, so the client can choose its text colour and how much tint to add for text to stay readable. It is meant to be used together with a background effect (blur) on the same surface, but doesn't require one.
Rikkiti OS uses it for the panel's glass levels (docs/panel-v2-plan.md §3.6) through the Baldr toolkit (docs/baldr-requests/038), since version 2 for text drawn straight on the desktop (docs/baldr-requests/212), and since version 3 cell by cell, so each piece of that text can read what is behind it (docs/baldr-requests/213).

interface.name: rikkiti_backdrop_manager_v1
interface.description: A global the client binds to ask about the backdrops of its surfaces.

entry.name: backdrop_exists
entry.summary: the surface already has a rikkiti_backdrop_v1 object

request.name: destroy
request.description: Existing rikkiti_backdrop_v1 objects are not affected.

request.name: get_backdrop

description.summary: watch the backdrop behind a surface

request.description: Creates an object that reports the brightness of what is behind the surface. A surface may have only one; asking for a second is the backdrop_exists error.

interface.name: rikkiti_backdrop_v1

description.summary: the brightness of the backdrop behind one surface

interface.description:
Reports the relative luminance of the content that shows through the surface: whatever the compositor renders below it within the surface's own bounds (for a popup, the popup's, not its parent's), after the blur the surface's background effect applies (or a comparable blur when there is none, unless the client asked for measure_as_shown), before the surface's own pixels.
Luminance is relative luminance as used by WCAG contrast (linear-light sRGB, weighted 0.2126 R, 0.7152 G, 0.0722 B), scaled so 0 is black and 65535 is white.
The compositor sends a luminance event soon after the object is created and the surface is mapped, and again whenever the backdrop changes enough to matter: the wallpaper changes, a window moves or appears behind the surface, the surface moves, is resized or is re-anchored, a workspace switches. It should not send more than about four events a second for one surface. While the backdrop is animating it may wait and send only the settled values.
When the surface is unmapped, no events are sent until it is mapped again.

request.name: destroy
request.description: No more events are sent for this surface.

event.name: luminance
event.description: The darkest, average and brightest luminance of the blurred backdrop (or, after measure_as_shown, the backdrop as it shows) behind the surface, sampled over its bounds at a resolution the compositor chooses (cells of about 10 to 20 logical pixels are enough). A client that needs text to read everywhere on the surface checks its colours against min and max.

request.name: measure_as_shown

description.summary: report the backdrop without the blur

request.description: From now on, the backdrop is measured as it shows, without any blur: for a surface whose own pixels sit straight on what is behind it (text on the desktop), where the contrast that matters is at the size of a letter, which a blur hides. The cells are still averaged, but about the size of a letter (around 6 logical pixels), so a patch as wide as a letter is seen rather than lost in a cell it half covers. A luminance event follows with the new values. There is no way back short of destroying the object.

request.name: watch_map

description.summary: also report the backdrop cell by cell

request.description:
From now on the backdrop also comes as a map: its brightness cell by cell over the part of the surface that is on screen, measured as the luminance event's numbers are (blurred, or as shown after measure_as_shown), in the same cells. One min/avg/max can't serve text over a wallpaper that runs from light to dark under it; with the map, each piece of text can take the colour that reads over what is behind that piece.
A map is map_begin, then map_rows until every row has come, then map_done. One follows soon after this request, and another whenever the map changes enough to matter, at the same pace as the luminance events (with one, or alone when only the map moved).

event.name: map_begin

description.summary: a map of the backdrop starts

event.description: The map's size and where it lies on the surface: columns × rows cells of `cell` logical pixels square (the last column and row may be cut short by the edge), the first cell's top-left corner at x, y in surface-local logical pixels (not 0, 0 when the surface is partly off screen: only what is shown is measured).

arg.name: cell
arg.summary: a cell's side, in logical pixels

arg.name: x
arg.summary: the map's left edge, surface-local logical pixels

arg.name: y
arg.summary: the map's top edge, surface-local logical pixels

event.name: map_rows
event.description: Rows first_row onward, `columns` bytes each, as many whole rows as the array holds. A byte is a cell's relative luminance written as the 8-bit sRGB grey of the same brightness: 0 is black, 255 white, and a client wanting WCAG luminance decodes it with the sRGB curve.

arg.name: first_row
arg.summary: the first row in this event

arg.name: cells
arg.summary: columns bytes per row, row after row

event.name: map_done
event.description: Every row of the map started by the last map_begin has been sent.
